Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Rural police stations (police/gendarmerie brigades) in Burkina Faso record case files, complaints, and incident reports using handwritten procès-verbaux (PVs), as mandated by the Criminal Procedure Code (Loi n°040-2019/AN). Officers draft originals and certified copies, signed per page, and transmit physically to prosecutors—no digital specification at station level. Official police site describes in-person filing at stations open 7/7, triggering procedures without digital mention. Digitisation limited to urban courts (e.g., e-criminal records in Ouagadougou/Bobo/Tenkodogo via UNDP) and recent online filing platforms (justice-penale.gov.bf, 2025)—not initial rural recording. Francophone norms and lack of rural digital evidence confirm paper-based. No pilots or aggregate entry found for rural police. Criminal Procedure Code, Police.gov.bf, UNDP RoLHR.

revision_notes: Original score 1 (Entirely paper) confirmed. Cited sources (Criminal Procedure Code, police.gov.bf, UNDP RoLHR) verified as relevant and describe paper-based PV recording at station level. Fresh search found evidence of a planned 'main courante informatisée' platform (Ministry of Territorial Administration), around 80% complete as of December 2023 and intended to digitise commissariat/gendarmerie brigade registers nationally, but no confirmation was found that it has become operational or reached rural stations as of late 2025; recent (November 2025) ministry reporting on rural security reorganisation makes no mention of record digitisation. Score remains 1.
revised_comments: Rural police stations and gendarmerie brigades in Burkina Faso record incidents, complaints and case files (procès-verbaux) by hand, in line with the Criminal Procedure Code (Loi n°040-2019/AN); officers draft signed paper originals and copies that are physically transmitted to prosecutors. The Ministry of Territorial Administration's planned 'main courante informatisée' platform, intended to replace paper incident registers at commissariats and gendarmerie brigades nationally, had reached roughly 80% completion by late 2023 and was expected to become operational in early 2024, but there is no confirmed evidence that it has reached rural stations at the point of data capture. Digital tools that do exist, such as the gendarmerie's 'Ma Gendarmerie' application and Brigade Numérique, serve citizen alerting and open-source intelligence functions rather than case-record data capture. Recent reorganisation of rural security provision (2024-2025) has focused on redeploying gendarmerie units to rural communes rather than on digitising records. Data capture at rural facilities therefore remains entirely paper-based.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Burkina Faso operates a national Education Management Information System (SIGE/EMIS) for education statistics, rated acceptable (3/4) by ECOWAS standards, based on annual school census data ADEA report. School census questionnaires feed into EMIS UNESCO IIEP. No evidence found of digital tools for direct data entry in rural primary schools for attendance, enrollment, or grades. Analogous rural health facilities use paper forms later digitized into DHIS2, with parallel digital pilots not replacing paper BMJ study. Limited pilots like FIUE-BF student database exist but not widespread in rural areas Gov site. Rural schools predominantly paper-based, data aggregated/digitized at district level: score 2.

revision_notes: Original score 1 (Entirely paper) confirmed, despite an internal inconsistency in the original Comments text which referenced 'score 2' - the Value Code recorded was 1 and the evidence supports 1, not 2. Cited sources (ADEA EMIS peer review, IIEP EiE article) verified as relevant. Fresh search found the 2023/2024 national primary school census methodology (published September 2024), which confirms data collection at school level is via paper 'fiches' completed by school directors, with digital entry occurring only at CEB/regional level (STATEDUC 2 application). The FIUE-BF student-identification pilot (Boulgou and Kourwéogo provinces only) likewise collects data on paper at school level, with digital entry performed by dedicated enrolment agents away from the classroom. No evidence found of digital data capture at the rural school facility itself. Score confirmed at 1.
revised_comments: Data capture in Burkina Faso's rural primary schools remains entirely paper-based. The Ministry of Basic Education's annual primary school census (Annuaire Statistique) for the 2023/2024 school year confirms that school directors complete paper forms during a fixed statistical collection day, which are then physically routed through Circonscriptions d'Education de Base and Regional Education Directorates, where staff enter the data into the STATEDUC 2 application at district or regional level. A pilot student-identification platform (FIUE-BF), covering only two provinces (Boulgou and Kourwéogo) as of the 2023/2024 school year, likewise relies on paper collection tools completed at school level, with digital entry performed by dedicated CEB/DPEPS enrolment agents rather than at the school itself. No evidence indicates rural primary schools capture attendance, enrolment or grade data digitally at the point of collection.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics (CSPS) in Burkina Faso predominantly use paper-based recording for patient data and service volumes. Health workers summarize indicators on paper forms monthly, submitted to districts for entry into national DHIS2/Endos system; digital entry occurs at district level, not point-of-care.BMJ Global Health study. Digital pilots exist, e.g., REC-Maternity/IeDA tablet app for maternal/child consultations, deployed in >1,600 CSPS across select districts (556 by 2022), recording millions of visits but running parallel to paper without integration, causing dual burden and discrepancies.BMJ Global Health study; MoH site. No evidence of majority rural CSPS using digital routinely; EMRs limited to pilots/incomplete, absent at primary level.BMC study. Barriers: poor integration, infrastructure (power/connectivity), training, fragmentation (35+ DHIs, 66% pilots). National ambition (e.g., e-sante strategy) outpaces rural reality of paper default.

revision_notes: Original score 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) confirmed. Cited sources (BMJ Global Health REC-Maternity/IeDA study, MoH site) verified as relevant and support the score. Fresh searches found a 2024 BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making study confirming physical consultation registers remain the predominant data-collection instrument nationally, and a 2025 BMC Health Services Research study confirming decentralised tablet-based data entry is used at facility level only in specific pilot districts (e.g. Yako), alongside continued paper-based entry elsewhere. A 2025/2026 BMJ Global Health evaluation of REC-Maternity in Toma and Gourcy districts found the digital tool operates in parallel with paper registers, with limited data agreement between the two and evidence of a double reporting burden. Score confirmed at 2.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics (CSPS) in Burkina Faso predominantly record patient consultations and service data on paper registers, which health workers summarise monthly onto paper reporting forms for onward transmission to district teams who enter the data into DHIS2. Digital point-of-care tools exist but remain limited to specific pilot districts: the REC-Maternity tablet application, evaluated across 34-36 facilities in Toma and Gourcy districts, and decentralised tablet-based nutrition data entry piloted in Yako district, both run in parallel with, rather than replacing, paper registers, and studies through 2024-2025 found only partial data agreement between the digital and paper records, reflecting a persistent dual-recording burden. The great majority of rural CSPS nationally continue to rely on paper as the primary data-capture medium, with digital tools present only on a pilot basis.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices in Burkina Faso predominantly use paper-based systems for birth registration, requiring manual transcription into duplicate registers, with copies sent to courts annually. Parents must travel long distances (up to 600km, 3-4 days) to these offices, contributing to low timely registration rates (74% rural vs 93% urban). The iCivil digital system, using smartphone apps and bubble-code wristbands, enables digital notification and registration primarily at ~130/2584 points (~5%), mostly health facilities (104) and some community sites (16), including rural areas, sending data via SMS to a national digital register. Parents can then retrieve certificates at any office. However, legal framework still recognizes only paper registers; digital revision pending. No evidence majority of rural registries (~80% population rural) use digital at point-of-service; iCivil is donor-supported expansion/pilot, not standard. Barriers: poor infrastructure, illiteracy, insecurity, low coverage. National ambition for full digital CRVS exists, but rural reality lags with paper default and digital in isolated projects. CRVS Systems; African Union; UNFPA

revision_notes: Original score 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) confirmed. Cited sources (CRVS Systems iCivil webinar, AU CRVS modernisation document, UNFPA) verified as relevant and describe a predominantly paper-based rural registration system with iCivil operating at only a small share of notification points. Fresh search found a June 2025 report on 2024 execution of the 2023-2025 National Civil Registration Strategy: 22 main civil registry centres were networked and roughly 3.39 million archival records from 54 communes were digitised during 2024, alongside continued paper-based registration nationally and a legal framework that as of 2024/2025 still recognises only paper registers as authoritative. This confirms digitisation remains partial and non-standard. Score confirmed at 2.
revised_comments: Civil registration at the point of service in rural Burkina Faso is predominantly paper-based: birth and death events are recorded in physical duplicate registers, with parents in remote areas sometimes travelling several days to reach a registration office, contributing to a rural birth registration rate (74%) below the urban rate (93%). The government's iCivil digital notification system, using smartphone applications and bubble-tag wristbands linked to a national digital register, operates at only around 130 of 2,584 vital-event notification points nationally (predominantly in health facilities, with a small number of community sites), and death registration has not yet been digitised. Under the 2023-2025 National Civil Registration Strategy, 22 main civil registry centres were networked and some 3.39 million archival civil-status records from 54 communes were digitised and secured during 2024, alongside continued paper-based registration at most rural offices. The legal framework as of 2024/2025 still recognises only physical registers, with a revision to give digital registers equal legal standing still pending before parliament. Digital data capture therefore remains present only on a limited, non-standard basis alongside a predominantly paper system.
